findings.title: The augmented-model recursions omit the continuous-state-dependent switch likelihood
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2006__accepted__v7-barber06a-01 — The augmented-model recursions omit the continuous-state-dependent switch likelihood
findings.markdown:
**Exact locations.** PDF page 4 (journal page 2518), Equation (5) and the claim that the conditional forward component is Gaussian; PDF page 5, Algorithm 1; PDF page 8 (2522), Equation (11), its following paragraph and footnote 8. The affected scope is stated in the abstract on PDF page 1, the augmented joint model on page 2, the assumed-density-filtering interpretation on page 3 and Figure 2 on page 4. The relaxed-EC discussion on page 11 does not correct the missing factor.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** The method is advertised for the augmented SLDS, where the switch at time \(t+1\) depends on the preceding continuous state \(h_t\). Its continuous dynamics and emissions are conditionally linear Gaussian. The abstract identifies projection to a Gaussian mixture as the central approximation, with a separate, optional backward conditional-independence approximation. Figure 2 describes propagation using the exact dynamics before collapse, and page 3 calls the forward procedure assumed density filtering. These claims require the continuous component passed to Gaussian projection to include the switch likelihood.

**Error.** Write

\[
g_{s'}(h,s)=p(s_{t+1}=s'\mid h_t=h,s_t=s).
\]

The augmented joint model on page 2 gives

\[
p(h_t,h_{t+1}\mid s_t=s,s_{t+1}=s',v_{1:t})
=
\frac{
 p(h_{t+1}\mid h_t,s')\,
 g_{s'}(h_t,s)\,
 p(h_t\mid s,v_{1:t})
}{
 \int g_{s'}(h,s)p(h\mid s,v_{1:t})\,dh
}.
\]

Equation (11) instead omits the gate \(g_{s'}\) and its normalizer. Its footnote explicitly asserts that the next switch carries no additional information about the current continuous state. The augmented model has a direct \(h_t\to s_{t+1}\) edge, so that assertion is false. Conditioning on the next switch generally tilts the Gaussian continuous distribution into a non-Gaussian distribution.

Algorithm 1 averages the gate into a scalar component weight but uses the ordinary, un-tilted LDS Gaussian for its continuous moments. Averaging the switch probability does not supply the missing gate-weighted moments. The same factor is missing from the reverse conditional used for LDSBACKWARD; with a state-dependent gate, that reverse conditional is generally not the linear Gaussian assumed on page 8.

### Exact three-step counterexample

Let there be two switch states, written \(s_t\in\{-1,+1\}\), one hidden dimension and one observed dimension. Choose

\[
\begin{aligned}
&s_1\text{ uniform},\qquad h_1\mid s_1\sim N(0,1),\\
&h_{t+1}=\tfrac9{10}h_t+\eta_t,
\qquad \eta_t\sim N(0,\tfrac1{100}),\\
&p(s_{t+1}=+1\mid h_t,s_t)=\Phi(10h_t),\\
&v_t=s_t+\epsilon_t,
\qquad \epsilon_t\sim N(0,\tfrac1{16}),
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF, and noises are independent. Thus \(A(s)=9/10\), \(B(s)=0\), the emission biases are \(\pm1\), and every prior/process/observation covariance is strictly positive. The dynamics are stable. The gate is smooth, strictly between zero and one at every finite hidden state, and is permitted by the paper's unrestricted augmented transition model. The switch need not depend nontrivially on its previous discrete state. Observe

\[
(v_1,v_2,v_3)=(0,1,-1/50).
\]

In the printed forward algorithm, all Gaussian component means remain zero: the emissions have \(B=0\), so observations cannot change those means. The exact scalar gate average in Equation (7) is always \(1/2\) by symmetry. This remains true even if every mixture component is retained and no collapse is performed. Consequently, the algorithm treats the final switch prior as uniform and reports

\[
\widetilde p(s_3=+1\mid v_{1:3})
=\frac1{1+\exp(16/25)}
=0.34524653939368\ldots.
\]

At the final time, the smoothed posterior equals the filtered posterior, so no backward pass can repair this result.

The exact answer is elementary. Represent each probit gate by an independent auxiliary standard normal variable. The two gate variables are jointly Gaussian with variances \(101\) and \(83\), covariance \(90\), and correlation

\[
r=\frac{90}{\sqrt{8383}}=0.9829756876\ldots.
\]

For centered bivariate normals, rotational symmetry gives positive-orthant probability

\[
c=p(s_2=+1,s_3=+1)
=\frac14+\frac{\arcsin r}{2\pi}.
\]

The likelihood ratio of \(v_2=1\) under the negative versus positive state is \(e^{-32}\); \(v_1=0\) is uninformative. Hence, before the final observation,

\[
q=p(s_3=+1\mid v_1=0,v_2=1)
=\frac12+\tanh(16)\frac{\arcsin r}{\pi}
=0.94118095383091\ldots.
\]

The final observation multiplies positive-state odds by \(e^{-16/25}\). Therefore,

\[
p(s_3=+1\mid v_{1:3})
=\frac{q e^{-16/25}}{1-q+q e^{-16/25}}
=0.89403818597357\ldots.
\]

The printed algorithm has absolute posterior error \(0.5487916466\ldots\) and selects the opposite MAP switch. Positive observation densities and continuity make the opposing decisions persist on an open set of observations; this is not a zero-probability equality or tie case.

The discrepancy already appears before any smoothing or mixture reduction. At time 2, the exact conditional mean is

\[
E[h_2\mid s_2=+1,v_{1:2}]
=\frac9{10}\frac{10\sqrt{2/\pi}}{\sqrt{101}}
=0.71453233034389\ldots,
\]

while the algorithm supplies zero. Moment-matching projection to one Gaussian would preserve this mean. Retaining more of its identical centered Gaussian components cannot recover it.

The zero observation loading is not essential. The executable check repeats exact path integration with \(B(s)=0.001\) and \(0.01\), both full-rank in one dimension. Exact final positive-state probabilities are respectively \(0.8930295\) and \(0.8847668\), versus \(0.3453193\) and \(0.3514101\) from the untruncated printed forward method. Every case still selects the wrong MAP switch.

### Reproducible evidence

Run:

The script evaluates the closed-form witness at 70-digit precision. Independently, it enumerates all eight switch paths, performs ordinary Gaussian conditioning conditional on each path, and integrates the two remaining probit gate factors using a bivariate Gaussian orthant integral. That calculation agrees with the closed form to below \(10^{-12}\); reported quadrature error is below \(8\times10^{-14}\). It separately implements Algorithm 1 without any component reduction and with exact analytic gate averaging, ruling out finite sampling and mixture-collapse explanations.

As a control, ordinary single-state LDS filtering and RTS smoothing at lengths 3, 10 and 30 agree with independent dense Gaussian conditioning within \(4.5\times10^{-16}\). The error is specific to the omitted augmented gate, not an incorrect interpretation of the ordinary Gaussian routines.

 Critical original renders are an unpublished audit file, an unpublished page image, an unpublished page image, an unpublished page image, an unpublished page image, an unpublished page image, and an unpublished page image.

**Discovery method.** Traced conditioning under the explicit augmented joint distribution and noticed that the direct hidden-state-to-next-switch edge disappears from Equations (5) and (11). Designed a persistent latent-state model whose previous switch observation informs the next switch entirely through that missing edge.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original rendered equations and their footnotes, the abstract and assumed-density-filtering description, all later qualifications and Appendices A–E. Derived the Gaussian orthant answer analytically; independently enumerated all switch paths with numerical orthant integration and compared an untruncated translation of the printed forward recursion. Checked positive covariances, stable dynamics, smooth gate, nonzero-loading perturbations and the ordinary LDS control. A separate skeptical review inspected original PDF pages 1–5, 8 and 11 and full-resolution critical renders, then independently rederived the 70-digit correlation, exact posterior, printed posterior and conditional mean. Its values agree and are preserved in `root-independent-check.json`. This was a targeted independent verification, not a second full-paper review.

**Why it matters.** This is not merely a poor example for an explicitly unconstrained approximation. A central advertised extension to continuous-state-dependent switches is derived using a conditional-independence identity that contradicts that very model. The algorithm discards gate information before its stated Gaussian projection, fails to preserve even first moments, and remains wrong without mixture truncation or the optional backward independence assumption. Correcting it requires rederiving gate-weighted non-Gaussian forward moments and reverse conditionals, with additional integration or approximation, or withdrawing the augmented-model claim. A scalar normalizer, more mixture components, more accurate gate averaging or the discussed relaxed EC does not fix the omission. Ordinary SLDS smoothing remains a contribution; the specific augmented-model inference justification is false.

**Limits.** The paper explicitly identifies all outputs as approximations and discusses forward/backward inconsistency on page 11. Those disclosures concern Gaussian collapse and the different optional backward assumption; they do not identify the missing augmented gate. The witness refutes the claimed derivation and scope, not a universal numerical-accuracy theorem that the paper never states. It does not demonstrate that the historical augmented experiments in Figure 8 had incorrect reported scores, nor invalidate the ordinary SLDS comparisons or Table 2. The original software and experimental driver were not recovered through bounded primary-source routes; failed retrieval is not evidence for this issue.

**Confidence:** High. The missing factor follows directly from Bayes' rule, and the exact posterior discrepancy persists with smooth gates, strictly positive variances, stable dynamics and nonzero observation loadings.

findings.markdown:
The cost critic used by the proposed control algorithm can freeze an interior policy that has a strictly improving conditioned-cost direction.

**Exact location.** PDF pages 9–10 (printed 1945–1946), Section 3.1, initialization of $Y_i(0)=0$ and updates (7)–(8); PDF page 11 (printed 1947), their synchronous versions (11)–(12); PDF page 13 (printed 1949), the assertion $\|Y_i(n)-\hat J(\bar\theta(n))\|\to0$ and the projected-gradient ODE (14); PDF page 14 (printed 1950), the resulting convergence to Kuhn–Tucker points/local minima. The intended control contribution is described in the abstract/introduction (PDF pages 1–5), problem definition (PDF pages 5–7), and conclusion (PDF page 23).

**Affected claim and assumptions.** The new adaptive algorithm is claimed to optimize long-run average cost conditioned on the rare event, with its policy updates asymptotically following the gradient of that conditioned average cost. The convergence discussion explicitly permits only local optimization; the counterexample below fails even first-order stationarity. Assumption (A) requires every stationary deterministic policy to induce an irreducible finite Markov chain. The cost $h$ is an arbitrary bounded function of current state, action and next state, and the rare-event threshold exceeds the original stationary mean under every deterministic policy. Assumption (B) requires the usual square-summable, nonsummable three-timescale step sizes. All these restrictions are satisfied below, as are aperiodicity, strictly positive transitions and a nondegenerate interior rare-event tilt.

**Reproducible counterexample.** Use three states and two actions $A,B$ at each state. Their transition rows are

$$
p(1,\cdot,A)=(3/5,1/5,1/5),\qquad
p(1,\cdot,B)=(1/5,3/5,1/5),
$$

and both actions at states 2 and 3 have row $(2/5,2/5,1/5)$. Set

$$
g(i,a)=\mathbf1\{i=3\},\quad \alpha=1/2,\quad
h(i,a,j)=\mathbf1\{i=2\}.
$$

Both functions are action independent and bounded. Every transition probability is at least $1/5$. Under every policy the next-state probability of state 3 is $1/5$, so the original stationary mean of $g$ is exactly $1/5<\alpha$. Let $\theta$ be the probability of action $A$ in state 1; the other two policy coordinates have no effect on any transition or cost. Then

$$
P_\theta=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/5+2\theta/5&3/5-2\theta/5&1/5\\
2/5&2/5&1/5\\
2/5&2/5&1/5
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For $z=e^\zeta$, the tilted matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,1,z)P_\theta$ has positive Perron eigenvector $(1,1,z)^T$ and eigenvalue $(4+z)/5$. Its logarithmic derivative is $z/(4+z)$, giving the unique finite optimum $z_*=4$, or $\zeta_*=\log4$, with second derivative $1/4$ and positive rate $\log(5/4)$. Applying the paper's own conditioned-transition formula (2) gives

$$
Q_\theta=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/8+\theta/4&3/8-\theta/4&1/2\\
1/4&1/4&1/2\\
1/4&1/4&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its stationary law is

$$
\eta_\theta=\left(\frac2{9-2\theta},\ \frac12-\frac2{9-2\theta},\ \frac12\right).
$$

Consequently the true conditioned average cost and its derivative are

$$
\hat J(\theta)=\frac12-\frac2{9-2\theta},\qquad
\hat J'(\theta)=-\frac4{(9-2\theta)^2}<0.
$$

The prescribed uniform initialization has $\theta(0)=1/2$, where $\hat J=1/4$ and $\hat J'=-1/16$. However, $h(1,a,j)=0$ for every $a,j$. Since Step 0 sets $Y_1(0)=0$, update (7) leaves $Y_1(n)=0$ on every sample path. Update (8) therefore leaves $\theta_1(n)=1/2$ on every sample path as well. The obvious $N_i$ versus $N_i-1$ perturbation-matrix dimension slip in Step 0 can be corrected charitably using the preceding definition; every valid perturbation sequence still gives this failure. This induction does not depend on estimation of the eigenvector or risk parameter, the transition proposals, the Hadamard signs, the positive step sizes, or the averaging length $L$. It applies to the synchronous versions too.

Thus the algorithm converges to a nonstationary interior policy, rather than the claimed projected-gradient/Kuhn–Tucker limit. The best deterministic policy has $\theta=1$ and conditioned cost $3/14$, so the limiting gap is $1/4-3/14=1/28$. The final output uses the perturbed policy: this does not resolve the error. For any $0<\delta\le1/4$, its state-1 probability is at most $3/4$, giving a gap at least $\hat J(3/4)-\hat J(1)=2/105$; as $\delta\to0$ the gap tends to $1/28$.

**Underlying error.** With a fixed policy and a positive sampling row $q(i,\cdot)$, the conditional mean of the cost observation in (7) is

$$
\sum_j q(i,j)h^\theta(i,j)\frac{p^\theta(i,j)}{q(i,j)}
=\sum_j p^\theta(i,j)h^\theta(i,j).
$$

This is a one-step, state-specific cost under the original row. It is not the stationary average cost under the conditioned chain. Irreducibility does not make these quantities equal. In the counterexample the three targets are $0,1,0$, whereas the true average at initialization is $1/4$. The displayed tracking assertion on PDF page 13 is therefore false. Merely deleting the importance ratio still leaves a state-specific immediate-cost critic and still freezes state 1 in this example.

**Discovery method.** Traced the advertised conditioned-cost gradient from the problem definition through the cost critic and policy update. Computed the critic's conditional drift, then constructed an action-independent bounded cost that is zero at the state whose policy changes the future conditioned occupancy.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the initialization, updates, tracking assertion, ODE and conclusion on rendered original PDF pages. The saved `check.py` uses exact rational/SymPy arithmetic to verify the Perron eigenpair, optimal tilt, conditioned kernel, stationary law, true gradient and both gaps. Its 20,000-transition run uses an ideal exact conditioned kernel and illustrates the invariant; the universal pathwise induction above is the proof and also covers estimated positive kernels. The full paper was read, including the later experiments and references after identifying the candidate. Root independently verified the full draft, the exact algebra and targeted original PDF pages 5–11 and 13–14 (including rendered pages 10, 11 and 13); this was a targeted second check, not a second full-paper review. This is not a historical-code or routing-experiment reconstruction.

**Why it matters.** Learning a control policy for the conditioned Markov chain is the paper's principal new contribution beyond prior conditional-performance estimation. Its actual cost critic can supply identically zero updates for a strictly improving interior policy coordinate, even with a perfectly regular rare event and ideal transition estimates. A new global-average or appropriate cost-to-go estimator and a corresponding policy-gradient/convergence analysis are required. This is not a constant, endpoint, step-size or local-versus-global qualification. The established fixed-policy Perron/conditioning facts and the possibility of the reported routing behavior are not refuted; no claim is made about an unavailable historical implementation or corrected numerical ranking.

**Confidence.** High. The failure is a pathwise algebraic invariant of the printed updates, and the nonzero gradient and gap are exact rational quantities for a strictly positive three-state model.

**Source/correction recheck.** The official article page and its GitHub directory list the paper and metadata, with no correction or implementation linked there. The author’s current publication list identifies the same article without a correction link. Searches for the exact title with correction/erratum/code terms did not locate a resolution. A repository-hosted preprint URL returned 404 over both HTTP and HTTPS. The cited Borkar–Juneja–Kherani conditioning paper was recovered directly from International Press after the DOI landing page was blocked; targeted pages 1–2 and 6–11 contain the fixed-policy conditioning/eigenvector simulation scheme, not a corrected version of this paper’s cost critic or policy update. The counterexample uses the conditioning formula itself, which checks exactly. These searches do not establish that no unpublished or differently hosted implementation exists.

With a fixed policy and a positive sampling row \(q(i,\cdot)\), the conditional mean of the cost observation in (7) is

findings.title: The clique-size stopping rule can approve a selected model whose Gaussian likelihood is unbounded
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2006__accepted__v7-castelo06a-01 — The clique-size stopping rule can approve a selected model whose Gaussian likelihood is unbounded
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 6, journal page 2626, final paragraph: a q-partial graph with largest clique smaller than the sample size is said to have a fittable Gaussian model and fittable submodels. Section 5.2, PDF pages 13–14, journal pages 2633–2634, defines the qp-clique diagnostic and says every point below the sample-size line corresponds to a model manageable by standard techniques. PDF page 17, journal page 2637, uses precisely this criterion to choose the threshold. The archived original implementation `qp 0.1-1`, `R/qp.R` lines 222–270, implements this maximum-clique criterion without checking positive-definite completion or likelihood existence.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** The procedure is advertised as reducing a p > n Gaussian structure-learning problem to a model and search space that ordinary Gaussian graphical-model methods can fit. The model class consists of arbitrary undirected graphs, not only decomposable graphs. PDF page 3 correctly calls full-rank clique covariances a necessary condition; pages 6 and 13–14 incorrectly use that condition as sufficient. Definition 1 allows q = 0, Section 5.1 requires q < n − 2, and PDF page 10 permits an arbitrarily specified common test level. The witness below uses the original code's default q = 0 and significance level 0.05. Every population covariance can be positive definite and faithful; the sample event has positive probability.

**Discovery method.** I traced the transition from the necessary clique-rank condition in Section 2 to the actual threshold-selection rule in Section 5.2. A cycle-supported positive-semidefinite likelihood recession direction suggested an exact counterexample. I then embedded the cycle in a larger sample so that the paper's actual t tests, at their default level, select the offending graph.

**Reproducible counterexample.** Take n = 29, p = 30 and q = 0. Define a 30 by 28 matrix U. Its first four rows are

\[
u_1=(1,0,0,\ldots,0),\quad
u_2=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,0,\ldots,0),\quad
u_3=(0,1,0,\ldots,0),\quad
u_4=(-1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,0,\ldots,0).
\]

Put

\[
a=99/100,\qquad b=\sqrt{199}/100,\qquad
h=\left(\frac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}}2,
          \frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}}2,0,\ldots,0\right).
\]

For j = 1,...,26, set \(u_{4+j}=a h+b e_{2+j}\). All rows have norm one and U has full column rank 28. Let Q be the 29 by 28 orthonormal Helmert contrast matrix, so \(Q^TQ=I\), \(\mathbf1^TQ=0\), and take the actual centered observations

\[
X=\sqrt{28}\,Q U^T.
\]

Their unbiased sample covariance is exactly \(S=X^TX/28=UU^T\). A covariance normalization by n instead of n − 1 changes none of the correlations or likelihood argument.

Among the four core vertices, the cycle edges 12, 23, 34, 41 have absolute sample correlation \(1/\sqrt2\), while 13 and 24 have correlation zero. Every nuisance vertex is correlated with every core vertex by an absolute amount at least

\[
r_{\min}=\frac{99}{100}\cos(3\pi/8)
          =0.3788565980414389\ldots,
\]

and distinct nuisance vertices have correlation \(a^2=0.9801\). For the paper's two-sided t test, df = n − q − 2 = 27. The 5% critical correlation is 0.36727768424..., below \(r_{\min}\). The script additionally bounds the weakest edge's exact two-sided p value, by rational interval arithmetic applied to the t27 integral, between 0.04269078032891 and 0.04269078032892. Thus every cycle or nuisance edge is rejected, while the two missing core pairs have p = 1 and are not rejected.

With q = 0 there is only one conditioning set. Consequently, every one of the 500 Monte Carlo tests gives the same result for a pair: estimated non-rejection rate zero on the retained edges and one on the two deleted pairs. Any threshold strictly between zero and one gives the same graph; for example \(\beta^*=0.949\), close to \(1-\alpha=0.95\). The graph is the join of a 26-vertex clique and a chordless four-cycle. It has 433 edges and largest clique size

\[
26+2=28<29=n.
\]

It therefore passes exactly the paper's qp-clique stopping rule, with all clique covariance matrices nonsingular. To see the latter directly, each maximal clique contains the 26 nuisance vertices and a core edge. The nuisance rows have distinct nonzero coordinates b in their last 26 coordinates, and the two core rows on an edge are linearly independent. Those 28 rows therefore have full rank.

Nevertheless, define a 30 by 30 matrix K0 with zeros outside its first four rows and columns, and core block

\[
K_C=\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt2&-1&0&1\\
-1&\sqrt2&-1&0\\
0&-1&\sqrt2&-1\\
1&0&-1&\sqrt2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its eigenvalues are \(0,0,2\sqrt2,2\sqrt2\), hence \(K_0\succeq0\), and direct multiplication gives \(K_0U=0\). Its only off-diagonal nonzeros are allowed cycle edges. Therefore, for every t ≥ 0, \(K_t=I+tK_0\) is an admissible positive-definite concentration matrix for the selected graph. But

\[
\operatorname{tr}(S K_t)=\operatorname{tr}(S),\qquad
\log\det K_t=2\log(1+2\sqrt2\,t)\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

The Gaussian log likelihood, apart from its positive multiplicative sample-size factor and constants, is \(\log\det K_t-\operatorname{tr}(SK_t)\). It is unbounded, so the claimed standard Gaussian maximum-likelihood fit does not exist. Equivalently, the specified covariance entries have no positive-definite completion: such a completion T would have \(\operatorname{tr}(T K_0)=\operatorname{tr}(S K_0)=0\), impossible for \(T\succ0\) and nonzero \(K_0\succeq0\).

**This is not an excluded, probability-zero sample.** The centered data have rank 28, the largest possible rank. Their two-dimensional nullspace varies continuously in a neighborhood. Writing a possible stress as \(VHV^T\), with V a continuous nullspace basis and H symmetric 2 by 2, the two forbidden entries impose two independent homogeneous linear constraints on H. At the displayed sample their solution is one-dimensional and positive definite up to a positive scale. Independence and positivity persist under small perturbations. All t-test decisions also have strict margins. Thus an open neighborhood of centered observations gives the same selected graph and a nonzero positive-semidefinite recession direction. For example, a sample from the positive-definite Gaussian \(N(0,I_{30})\), faithful to the empty concentration graph, enters this neighborhood with positive probability. The counterexample meets the paper's Gaussianity and faithfulness assumptions; it does not assert that a population q-partial graph must itself be this graph.

**Verification method.** `default-alpha.py` verifies the full default-level construction, centered sample, rank, exact stress product and eigenvalues, critical correlation, rationally enclosed t-tail probability, and the graph. Three hundred independent full-data perturbations preserve the graph, full sample rank, and positive stress. `check.py` independently verifies the smaller four-variable algebra, checks the q-partial graph propositions exhaustively on all 1,024 labelled five-vertex graphs at all four orders, and checks all three printed numerical tables with rounding allowances. All 30 original PDF pages, Appendix A, and the rendered critical pages were reviewed. The original CRAN source was inspected, not assumed absent. The root reviewer independently read original PDF pages 3, 6, 10, 13, 14 and 17, inspected the critical renders and original source, rederived the stress and determinant, and computed the weakest-edge p value independently at 70 digits. Its explicit nullspace calculation gives two independent forbidden-entry constraints and a positive-definite solution H with determinant 1/2, independently confirming the open-neighborhood argument. These targeted checks are preserved in `root-independent-check.json`; they are not represented as a second full-paper review.

**Significance and scope.** This is a failure of the procedure's advertised bridge from limited-order tests to a usable ordinary Gaussian-model search space. The actual stopping diagnostic approves a graph for which the likelihood objective has no maximizer. Full-rank clique statistics only characterize fit existence in special graph classes; they do not justify the arbitrary-graph proxy used here. Restoring this bridge requires a global positive-definite completion / likelihood-existence condition, or a graph-class restriction with a proved fitting criterion, and corresponding changes to threshold/model selection. The paper does not supply such a condition. The exact q-partial graph inclusion/separator results and the ability to compute non-rejection rates survive. I do not claim that any historical biological conclusion or published simulation score is false.

**Related corroboration, with an explicit limit.** The original archive includes the G1 n = 20, q = 10 sample covariance and stored 500-test output. Its threshold 0.95 graph exactly reproduces the paper's 4,574 retained edges and 97 wrongly removed edges. An independent clique enumeration gives size 14 rather than the printed 13; both are below n = 20, so this discrepancy does not change the gate decision. A numerical semidefinite calculation finds a supported nullspace stress positive on the 131-dimensional sample nullspace, with minimum positive eigenvalue about 0.00131 and support/annihilation residuals below 10^-7. This is strong numerical support that the concern is not confined to the constructed small-clique-gap family. It is not used as an exact historical nonexistence claim, because the archive contains rounded floating-point covariance entries and no raw observations or retained conditioning sets. `historical-stress.py`, its solver log, and results preserve this distinction.

**Confidence:** High. The technical consequence rests on an exact default-parameter counterexample and a positive-probability argument, independently of the historical numerical corroboration.

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2006__accepted__v7-demsar06a-01 — The recommended calibration does not hold under the stated classifier-equivalence null
findings.markdown:
The paper's central recommendation applies Friedman and its Nemenyi post-hoc procedure to equivalent classifiers evaluated on independent data sets without the within-data-set exchangeability condition needed by their null distributions. The following independent-data-set example has identical continuous score distributions, equal expected ranks, symmetric paired differences and a positive continuous joint density, yet the nominal 5% procedure rejects with probability greater than 11%. **The classical tests under their stronger joint-exchangeability null are not refuted.**

### Exact original scope and locations

- PDF page 2 defines the formal inputs: k algorithms, N data sets and one performance score for each algorithm/data-set pair. Scores are assumed reliable; the paper says it makes no other assumptions about the sampling scheme. This last sentence concerns the within-data-set estimation scheme, and is not misquoted here as an explicit denial of every possible distributional assumption.
- PDF page 5 says the sources of variation are independent data sets, unlike overlapping resamples within one data set. It says this avoids the elevated Type I error associated with within-data-set testing, and that the comparisons naturally give independent measurements. Those statements do not themselves establish exchangeability among classifiers within a data set.
- PDF page 11 defines the Friedman null: all algorithms are equivalent, and consequently their average ranks should be equal. It gives the chi-square statistic and the Iman–Davenport F transformation, with the rule of thumb N > 10 and k > 5 for the approximation.
- PDF pages 11–12 recommend Nemenyi all-pairs comparisons, with CD = q_alpha sqrt[k(k+1)/(6N)]. Table 5(a) gives q_.05 = 2.850 for six algorithms.
- PDF pages 16–18 and 27 explicitly acknowledge that different tests measure different aspects and that the empirical study does not estimate Type I/II errors. This finding does not attribute an empirical null-calibration experiment to the paper.
- PDF page 27 describes Wilcoxon/Friedman as safer methods that do not assume normality or homogeneity of variance, applicable to classification accuracy or other performance measures. No symmetry, within-data-set exchangeability, random assignment of classifier labels, or uniformity of rank permutations is stated anywhere in the full text. The prescribed reliable scores and independent data sets alone do not imply those properties.

### Counterexample with identical distributions, equal expected ranks and symmetric paired differences

Use k = 6 algorithms and N = 20 mutually independent data sets. Let

\[
c_j\in\{-5/6,-3/6,-1/6,1/6,3/6,5/6\},\qquad
F_c(x)=x+c x(1-x),\quad 0<x<1.
\]

Each F_c is a strictly increasing continuous CDF, since its derivative is at least 1 − |c| > 0. Let q_c be its inverse. For each data set independently draw U uniform on (0,1) and an independent fair sign S. Set the exact population performance score of algorithm j to

\[
C_j=\begin{cases}
q_{c_j}(U),&S=+1,\\
1-q_{c_j}(U),&S=-1.
\end{cases}
\]

Every algorithm has **exactly the same Uniform(0,1) marginal score distribution**, because

\[
\Pr(C_j\le x)=\tfrac12F_{c_j}(x)+\tfrac12[1-F_{c_j}(1-x)]=x.
\]

Thus all have identical means, medians, variances and every other marginal distributional characteristic. Every pairwise difference is symmetric about zero: flipping S reflects both scores and reverses the difference. Every pair wins with probability one half, and every algorithm's expected rank is 3.5. The data sets are independent, the scores are continuous and untied, and no noisy or biased score estimate is involved.

For fixed U, differentiating F_c(q_c(U)) = U gives

\[
\frac{\partial q_c(U)}{\partial c}
=-\frac{q_c(U)(1-q_c(U))}{1+c-2cq_c(U)}<0.
\]

The rank vector on each data set is therefore exactly (1,2,3,4,5,6) or its reverse, each with probability one half. This dependence among classifiers is **not** joint label exchangeability, even though their marginal performance distributions and expected ranks are identical. This distinction defines the scope of the finding.

If B of the N signs are positive, B is Binomial(N,1/2), and the average ranks satisfy

\[
R_j=\frac{B j+(N-B)(k+1-j)}N.
\]

Substituting into the paper's statistic gives exactly

\[
\chi_F^2=(k-1)\frac{(2B-N)^2}{N}.
\]

At B = 13, the statistic is 9, its F transformation is 1.879120879..., and the largest rank difference is 1.5. The omnibus p values exceed .05 and Nemenyi does not reject. At B = 14, the statistic is 16, its F transformation is 3.619047619..., and the largest rank difference is 2. The chi-square p value is .00684407 and the F p value is .00485470. The Nemenyi critical difference, even using the paper's rounded q = 2.850, is 1.68608..., so a pair is declared different. Both components reject for every more extreme B as well.

Consequently, the complete recommended omnibus-plus-Nemenyi procedure falsely distinguishes some algorithms under the identical-marginal/equal-expected-rank null precisely when B <= 6 or B >= 14. Its exact rejection probability is

\[
\frac{2\sum_{b=0}^6\binom{20}{b}}{2^{20}}
=\frac{15115}{131072}
=0.11531829833984375,
\]

more than twice the nominal .05 level. This example meets the paper's N > 10, k > 5 rule.

Nor is the discrepancy explained by a small-N chi-square/F approximation. As N grows, the statistic converges to (k−1)Z² rather than chi-square_(k−1). For k = 6 the omnibus-plus-Nemenyi rejection probability approaches approximately .1315744, not .05.

The scores can also be realized as actual classifier accuracies. Each problem has constant metadata (U,S), a covariate V uniform on (0,1), and label zero. Algorithm j reads the metadata and predicts zero iff V <= C_j(U,S). Its exact population accuracy is the displayed C_j. Such deliberately constructed classifiers are not a claim about the historical experiments; they demonstrate admissibility under the formal algorithm/data-set setup and may be evaluated arbitrarily reliably.

### The failure persists with a strictly positive continuous joint density

To avoid relying on the rank-one copula, perturb each score by independent circular triangular noise supported on plus or minus delta = 10^-7. Uniform marginals remain exactly uniform under circular noise. Independently for each data set, with probability lambda = .001 replace the whole vector by six independent uniforms. The resulting joint score law is absolutely continuous with a continuous density bounded below by lambda; marginal equality and symmetric paired differences remain exact.

Let epsilon = .0001. When U lies in [epsilon,1−epsilon], every original score lies in [a,1−a], where a = 6 epsilon / 11. The adjacent-score gap is at least

\[
\frac{2a(1-a)}{11}>9.9\times10^{-6}>2\delta.
\]

Thus these scores neither wrap at an endpoint nor change their ordering under the noise. On all 20 data sets having no independent-vector replacement and U in this interior interval, the exact preceding rejection event persists. The overall false-rejection probability has the rigorous lower bound

\[
\frac{15115}{131072}
[(1-.001)(1-.0002)]^{20}
=0.1125824351222488\ldots>.11.
\]

The event and its bound use rational arithmetic and strict score-gap inequalities, not a Monte Carlo estimate.

### Verification and limits

`rank-null.py` verifies the CDF cancellation symbolically, strict inverse ordering, the rank-statistic identity and all 21 exact binomial cases. It independently evaluates chi-square and F critical regions at 70 digits through incomplete gamma/beta definitions, uses exact rational arithmetic for the binomial probability and positive-density lower bound, and records the asymptotic discrepancy. `rank-null-results.json` preserves the output. Use k = 6 algorithms and N = 20 mutually independent data sets. Let

\[ c_j\in\{-5/6,-3/6,-1/6,1/6,3/6,5/6\},\qquad F_c(x)=x+c x(1-x),\quad 0<x<1. \]

Every algorithm has exactly the same Uniform(0,1) marginal score distribution, because

\[ \Pr(C_j\le x)=\tfrac12F_{c_j}(x)+\tfrac12[1-F_{c_j}(1-x)]=x. \]

Thus all have identical means, medians, variances and every other marginal distributional characteristic. Every pairwise difference is symmetric about zero: flipping S reflects both scores and reverses the difference. Every pair wins with probability one half, and every algorithm's expected rank is 3.5. The data sets are independent, the scores are continuous and untied, and no noisy or biased score estimate is involved.

For fixed U, differentiating \(F_c\)(\(q_c\)(U)) = U gives

\[ \frac{\partial q_c(U)}{\partial c} =-\frac{q_c(U)(1-q_c(U))}{1+c-2cq_c(U)}<0. \]

The rank vector on each data set is therefore exactly (1,2,3,4,5,6) or its reverse, each with probability one half. This dependence among classifiers is not joint label exchangeability, even though their marginal performance distributions and expected ranks are identical. This distinction defines the scope of the finding.

If B of the N signs are positive, B is Binomial(N,1/2), and the average ranks satisfy

\[ R_j=\frac{B j+(N-B)(k+1-j)}N. \]

**Exact location.** Original PDF page 13, Section 5.3.1, Equation (38c) and the immediately following convexity/feasibility assertion; page 14, Equations (40b)–(41); page 15, Algorithm 5.2 and Proposition 10. The guaranteed-convergence fallback is introduced on pages 9 and 12–13. Sparsity and standing assumptions are defined on pages 3–4.

**Scope limitation.** This is a counterexample to the arbitrary-boundary initialization explicitly authorized in Section 5.3.1. It is not an established failure of the particular projection initializer suggested by Algorithm 5.2 line 1. A targeted search of 2,500 positive 2×3 data sets, alternating norm-preserving nearest-boundary and Euclidean cone-boundary initializations, found no violation in up to seven H steps per data set. These negative checks neither prove the restricted initializer safe nor count as an additional error.

**Affected claim.** The sparsity-maximization algorithm (SMA) is claimed to generate feasible factors and to converge to a point satisfying the constrained NMF first-order conditions, providing the guaranteed-convergent alternative when the tangent-plane method oscillates. The failure concerns SMA; the separate tangent-plane method, ordinary nonnegative least-squares subproblems and reported empirical advantages of TPC are not refuted.

**Error.** The normalized Hoyer measure

\[
 s(x)=\frac{\sqrt n-\|x\|_1/\|x\|_2}{\sqrt n-1}
\]

is not convex. Its tangent is not a global lower bound. Maximizing the minimum of its rowwise affine approximations, as in Equation (38), can produce a row strictly inside the forbidden minimum-sparsity cone. The next step gives that row a zero trust-region radius and fixes it at the infeasible point. This happens after two exact iterations starting with every row on the required minimum-sparsity boundary. It is not a numerical optimization failure or merely a false intermediate convexity assertion.

**Reproducible construction.** Set \(m=r=2,n=3,W=I_2\),

\[
 V=\begin{pmatrix}100&200&150\\3/10&3/10&3/10\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 H^0=\begin{pmatrix}2/3&1/3&1\\1/10&3/10&1/5\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Let \(s_h^{\min}=s(1,2,3)=(\sqrt3-6/\sqrt{14})/(\sqrt3-1)\approx0.1755115284\), \(s_h^{\max}=1\), \(s_w^{\min}=s(1,10^{-6})\), and \(s_w^{\max}=1\). Both initial rows have exactly the prescribed minimum sparsity. Section 5.3.1 explicitly permits starting with any point on the minimum boundary. Algorithm 5.2 line 1 suggests a more specific projection of the unconstrained solution; this particular rational initialization is not that suggested norm-preserving projection. The direct witness concerns the arbitrary-boundary initialization authorized by the prose. The negative checks of the suggested initializer are stated above. The initial and subsequent displayed factors have positive-definite Gram matrices; the certificate checks their determinants. The upper-bound constraints impose just nonnegativity when the maximum is 1. No fixed-factor-norm constraint appears in the original paper.

Grant the ordinary square-root correction when converting the squared objective bound (38b) to the SOCP in (39). The construction uses the intended \(\|V-H\|_F^2\le\|V-H^k\|_F^2\), so it does not rely on that separate transcription error.

The first Equation (38) optimum can be written explicitly. Put

\[
 a=89/3600,\quad b=8009/300,\quad
 R_0^2=\|V-H^0\|_F^2,
\]
\[
 T=\frac{b+\sqrt{b^2-4a(48000.27-R_0^2)}}{2a}
 \approx1662.28328956.
\]

Its unique factor is

\[
 H^{sp,0}=\begin{pmatrix}
 140-T/15&0&70+2T/15\\0&T/20&0
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]

To check global optimality, the two normalized sparsity gradients at \(H^0\) share a positive factor and reduce to coefficient rows \((-3,-12,6)\) and \((-40,20,-10)\). The objective maximizes their common lower level \(T\) over a nonnegative Euclidean ball centered at \(V\). The displayed active sets and positive multipliers \((T-600)/45\) and \((T-6)/400\) satisfy its KKT equations. The quadratic fixes the ball boundary. Strict convexity of the Euclidean projection for each level establishes uniqueness.

For each row \(p\), its exact distance from the minimum cone is

\[
 d(p)=\sqrt{6/7}\,\|p-(p^Te)e/3\|_2
       -\sqrt{1/7}\,(p^Te)/\sqrt3,
\]

when it is outside. Therefore the unique Equation (40) solution is its rowwise Euclidean-ball projection of \(V\). This gives

\[
 H^1\approx\begin{pmatrix}
68.1269112&109.9870371&213.7461776\\
.1618956&38.4233458&.1618956
\end{pmatrix},
\]

with row sparsities approximately \(0.2235906353\) and \(0.9885130449\), both feasible.

For the next Equation (38), write \(g_1=\nabla s(H^1_{1\bullet})\) and \(R_1=\|V-H^1\|_F\). Its unique optimum is

\[
 H^{sp,1}_{1\bullet}=V_{1\bullet}+R_1g_1/\|g_1\|_2,
 \qquad H^{sp,1}_{2\bullet}=V_{2\bullet}=(.3,.3,.3).
\]

The row-1 Cauchy–Schwarz bound proves this is the highest achievable level over the whole objective ball. Row 2 is inactive: its affine constraint has certified slack greater than 0.6288. The factor is nonnegative. Numerically,

\[
 H^{sp,1}\approx\begin{pmatrix}
5.7933202&149.0431845&206.2470843\\.3&.3&.3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The second row has sparsity exactly zero. Its distance to \(C(s_h^{\min})\) is zero, so Equation (40b) requires that it stay exactly uniform. The next full iterate is

\[
 H^2\approx\begin{pmatrix}
49.7154170&172.8008436&180.0229366\\.3&.3&.3
\end{pmatrix},
\]

whose row sparsities are approximately \(0.2048970340\) and **0**, respectively. Thus an initially feasible run produces an infeasible full iterate.

This cannot be dismissed as an overshoot fixed by taking a smaller stopping tolerance. At a positive uniform row, \(s=0\) and \(\nabla s=0\). All later first-step problems therefore have \(t\le0\). Selecting \(H^{sp}=H^k,t=0\) is a valid global optimizer, because every other row has nonnegative sparsity and the current objective level is allowed. The second step then fixes the uniform row forever by radius zero. Changes to \(W\) do not change this rowwise fact: the current factor remains in its current objective level set. Every later H-block output or cluster point of this permitted selection violates the minimum-sparsity condition. This establishes the fixed-W feasibility failure directly. The uniform H row is also preserved by the same permitted H-block selection when W changes, but no unproved assertion that a complete infinite alternating sequence retains all full-rank assumptions is needed for the direct counterexample. Even without that continuation, an ordinary positive objective tolerance between the first and second objective decreases makes the actual subroutine return the infeasible \(H^2\); scaling the data and factors scales those differences to any desired practical tolerance.

**Standing assumptions.** The Gram and strict sparsity-interval assumptions are met. The fixed-W level set used throughout this counterexample is a bounded Euclidean ball centered at V; its strict convexity follows from W=I. A strictly feasible full-rank point exists: take W columns (1,5×10^−7) and (5×10^−7,1), and H rows (1,2,5) and (5,2,1). Both W and H are strictly positive, and all their sparsities lie strictly between their respective minimum and maximum bounds. Thus the nonempty-interior condition is met. Joint W,H level sets are generally scale-unbounded, but that independent proof overstatement is not used as a finding here. The essentiality assumption also holds. Removing minimum constraints gives zero error through \(W=I,H=V\). Suppose any zero-error factorization satisfies \(s_w^{\min}=s(1,10^{-6})\). Each nonnegative column must have minor/major coordinate ratio at most \(10^{-6}\). The columns cannot both point toward the same coordinate, because all column ratios of \(V\) lie between 333 and 667, whereas such a pair would force ratios below \(10^{-6}\) or above \(10^6\). After permutation and harmless column scaling, write

\[
 W=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\a&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad0\le a,b\le10^{-6}.
\]

Then one row of \(H\) is proportional to \(V_{2\bullet}-aV_{1\bullet}\). Its 1-norm is at least 0.89955 and its 2-norm is at most \(\sqrt{.27}\). Its sparsity is therefore at most 0.001183013, strictly below \(s_h^{\min}\). Thus every otherwise globally optimal factorization violates a minimum constraint, as required. All matrices in the witness are nonnegative, and the displayed Gram determinants are strictly positive.

**Discovery method.** Audited the feasibility argument linking the linearized normalized sparsity objective to the reverse-convex cone. A targeted analytic search for two-row max-min SOCP steps identified the loss of feasibility; the construction was simplified to rational data and exact initial boundary points.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original rendered Equations (38)–(41), Algorithm 5.2, assumptions and Proposition 10. Derived the first optimizer from explicit KKT equations and the second from the support function of an Euclidean ball. `certify-sma.py` verifies all strict signs, rank conditions, cone distances and the essentiality bound using exact Fraction interval arithmetic with outward 150-bit square-root bounds. `certified-sma-results.json` records the checked values. `uniform-sma.py` separately reproduces the trace using the analytic nearest-point solution, not a generic SOCP solver. Neither check is a rerun of the historical experiments. Root independently re-derived the initial gradients and a 90-digit analytic trace, reran the exact certificate, and inspected the targeted original assumptions and algorithm pages; see `root-independent.py` and `root-independent-results.json`. This was targeted verification, not a second full-paper review.

**Repair and scope.** The paper's main framework includes a specifically advertised guaranteed-convergent sparse NMF method, offered as the reliable replacement for an oscillating method. Its actual convex subproblems can instead violate the defining sparsity constraint and admit permanently infeasible continuations. Replacing the normalized \(s\) in (38) by the convex margin \(G(x)=\|x\|_2-\|x\|_1/c_{n,s^{\min}}\) would alter the max-min objective to a scale-dependent quantity and require a corresponding algorithm and convergence analysis; it is not the normalized sparsity optimization stated in the paper. The same normalized objective and false convexity claim recur in the authors' primary ECCV 2006 paper, Equations (12)–(13), so the discrepancy is not a lone ambiguous symbol. The demonstrated error requires withdrawing or replacing the general boundary-start SMA feasibility guarantee as written. Restricting initialization could conceivably preserve a narrower method; the absence of a replacement proof is not evidence that such a restricted method is false. The defect does not establish that reported historical TPC results, the suggested projection initializer, or every NMF algorithm is invalid.

**Confidence.** High. Exact interval certificates, independent 90-digit derivations and original-page checks agree. Confidence is confined to the stated arbitrary-boundary SMA; the narrower projection-initialized version remains unrefuted.

To check global optimality, the two normalized sparsity gradients at \(H^0\) share a positive factor and reduce to coefficient rows \((-3,-12,6)\) and \((-40,20,-10)\). The objective maximizes their common lower level \(T\) over a nonnegative Euclidean ball centered at \(V\). The displayed active sets and positive multipliers \((T-600)/45\) and \((T-6)/400\) satisfy its KKT equations. The quadratic fixes the ball boundary. Strict convexity of the Euclidean projection for each level establishes uniqueness.

For each row \(p\), its exact distance from the minimum cone is

\[ d(p)=\sqrt{6/7}\,\|p-(p^Te)e/3\|_2 -\sqrt{1/7}\,(p^Te)/\sqrt3, \]

when it is outside. Therefore the unique Equation (40) solution is its rowwise Euclidean-ball projection of \(V\). This gives

\[ H^1\approx\begin{pmatrix} 68.1269112&109.9870371&213.7461776\\ .1618956&38.4233458&.1618956 \end{pmatrix}, \]

with row sparsities approximately \(0.2235906353\) and \(0.9885130449\), both feasible.

For the next Equation (38), write \(g_1=\nabla s(H^1_{1\bullet})\) and \(R_1=\|V-H^1\|_F\). Its unique optimum is

\[ H^{sp,1}_{1\bullet}=V_{1\bullet}+R_1g_1/\|g_1\|_2, \qquad H^{sp,1}_{2\bullet}=V_{2\bullet}=(.3,.3,.3). \]

The row-1 Cauchy–Schwarz bound proves this is the highest achievable level over the whole objective ball. Row 2 is inactive: its affine constraint has certified slack greater than 0.6288. The factor is nonnegative. Numerically,

\[ H^{sp,1}\approx\begin{pmatrix} 5.7933202&149.0431845&206.2470843\\.3&.3&.3 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The second row has sparsity exactly zero. Its distance to \(C(s_h^{\min})\) is zero, so Equation (40b) requires that it stay exactly uniform. The next full iterate is

\[ H^2\approx\begin{pmatrix} 49.7154170&172.8008436&180.0229366\\.3&.3&.3 \end{pmatrix}, \]

whose row sparsities are approximately \(0.2048970340\) and 0, respectively. Thus an initially feasible run produces an infeasible full iterate.

This cannot be dismissed as an overshoot fixed by taking a smaller stopping tolerance. At a positive uniform row, \(s=0\) and \(\nabla s=0\). All later first-step problems therefore have \(t\le0\). Selecting \(H^{sp}=H^k,t=0\) is a valid global optimizer, because every other row has nonnegative sparsity and the current objective level is allowed. Every later H-block output or cluster point of this permitted selection violates the minimum-sparsity condition. This establishes the fixed-W feasibility failure directly. The uniform H row is also preserved by the same permitted H-block selection when W changes, but no unproved assertion that a complete infinite alternating sequence retains all full-rank assumptions is needed for the direct counterexample. Even without that continuation, an ordinary positive objective tolerance between the first and second objective decreases makes the actual subroutine return the infeasible \(H^2\); scaling the data and factors scales those differences to any desired practical tolerance.

Standing assumptions. The Gram and strict sparsity-interval assumptions are met. The fixed-W level set used throughout this counterexample is a bounded Euclidean ball centered at V; its strict convexity follows from W=I. A strictly feasible full-rank point exists: take W columns (1,\(5\times10^{-7}\)) and (\(5\times10^{-7}\),1), and H rows (1,2,5) and (5,2,1). Both W and H are strictly positive, and all their sparsities lie strictly between their respective minimum and maximum bounds. Thus the nonempty-interior condition is met. Joint W,H level sets are generally scale-unbounded, but that independent proof overstatement is not used as a finding here. The essentiality assumption also holds. Removing minimum constraints gives zero error through \(W=I,H=V\). Suppose any zero-error factorization satisfies \(s_w^{\min}=s(1,10^{-6})\). Each nonnegative column must have minor/major coordinate ratio at most \(10^{-6}\). The columns cannot both point toward the same coordinate, because all column ratios of \(V\) lie between 333 and 667, whereas such a pair would force ratios below \(10^{-6}\) or above \(10^6\). After permutation and harmless column scaling, write

\[ W=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\a&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad0\le a,b\le10^{-6}. \]

Then one row of \(H\) is proportional to \(V_{2\bullet}-aV_{1\bullet}\). Its 1-norm is at least 0.89955 and its 2-norm is at most \(\sqrt{.27}\). Its sparsity is therefore at most 0.001183013, strictly below \(s_h^{\min}\). Thus every otherwise globally optimal factorization violates a minimum constraint, as required. All matrices in the witness are nonnegative, and the displayed Gram determinants are strictly positive.

Discovery method.

Audited the feasibility argument linking the linearized normalized sparsity objective to the reverse-convex cone. A targeted analytic search for two-row max-min SOCP steps identified the loss of feasibility; the construction was simplified to rational data and exact initial boundary points.

Verification method.

Rechecked the original rendered Equations (38)–(41), Algorithm 5.2, assumptions and Proposition 10. Derived the first optimizer from explicit KKT equations and the second from the support function of an Euclidean ball. certify-sma.py verifies all strict signs, rank conditions, cone distances and the essentiality bound using exact Fraction interval arithmetic with outward 150-bit square-root bounds. certified-sma-results.json records the checked values. uniform-sma.py separately reproduces the trace using the analytic nearest-point solution, not a generic SOCP solver. Neither check is a rerun of the historical experiments. Root independently re-derived the initial gradients and a 90-digit analytic trace, reran the exact certificate, and inspected the targeted original assumptions and algorithm pages; see root-independent.py and root-independent-results.json. This was targeted verification, not a second full-paper review.

Repair and scope.

The paper's main framework includes a specifically advertised guaranteed-convergent sparse NMF method, offered as the reliable replacement for an oscillating method. Its actual convex subproblems can instead violate the defining sparsity constraint and admit permanently infeasible continuations. Replacing the normalized \(s\) in (38) by the convex margin \(G(x)=\|x\|_2-\|x\|_1/c_{n,s^{\min}}\) would alter the max-min objective to a scale-dependent quantity and require a corresponding algorithm and convergence analysis; it is not the normalized sparsity optimization stated in the paper. The same normalized objective and false convexity claim recur in the authors' primary ECCV 2006 paper, Equations (12)–(13), so the discrepancy is not a lone ambiguous symbol. The demonstrated error requires withdrawing or replacing the general boundary-start SMA feasibility guarantee as written. Restricting initialization could conceivably preserve a narrower method; the absence of a replacement proof is not evidence that such a restricted method is false. The defect does not establish that reported historical TPC results, the suggested projection initializer, or every NMF algorithm is invalid.

Confidence.

High. Exact interval certificates, independent 90-digit derivations and original-page checks agree. Confidence is confined to the stated arbitrary-boundary SMA; the narrower projection-initialized version remains unrefuted.

### A single admissible distribution, kernel and regression function

Take n=1, X=[0,1], dρX(x)=p(x)dx with p(x)=2x, cρ=2, τ=1/8. Let

\[
x_j=2^{-j},\quad \ell_j=x_j/8,\quad a_j=2^{-4(j-1)},\quad
\psi(t)=\begin{cases}(1-t^2)^8,&|t|\le1,\\0,&|t|>1,\end{cases}
\qquad \phi_j(x)=a_j\psi((x-x_j)/\ell_j).
\]

The supports Ij=[7xj/8,9xj/8] are disjoint, with positive gaps. Define

\[
 K(x,t)=\sum_{j\ge1}\phi_j(x)\phi_j(t),\quad
 g(x)=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{\phi_j(x)}j,\quad
 f_\rho(x)=\int_0^xg(t)dt,\qquad Y=f_\rho(X)\text{ deterministically}.
\]

Every relevant assumption is satisfied:

* X is compact. The boundary-layer mass is 2s for 0<s≤1/2 and at most1 otherwise. Thus it is ≤4s^(1/2)=cρ²s^(4τ). Also p≤2 and |p(x)−p(v)|=2|x−v|≤2|x−v|^(1/8), as required by22–23.
* K is real, continuous, symmetric PSD: any finite quadratic form is a sum of squares. It has κ=sup sqrt(K(x,x))=1. There is no strict-positivity/universality assumption in the paper.
* The compact bump ψ is C7. On each product Ij×Ij, a mixed derivative of total order≤6 is bounded by a constant times a_j²ell_j^(-6)=O(x_j²). These derivatives therefore extend continuously by zero at the accumulation point and axes. K is in particular C3, even with three derivatives in each argument. The finite derivative conditions of Proposition9 hold.
* The nonzero functions φj form an orthonormal feature basis for HK: the coefficient map from ℓ² is injective because supports are disjoint. Hence g∈HK, with ||g||HK²=Σj^(-2)=π²/6<2.
* Since |ψ'|≤16 and maxj a_j/(jell_j)=16, ||g'||∞≤256. Thus fρ is C2 and Taylor condition35 holds with cρ'=128. The integral bound |fρ|≤Σ2ell_ja_j≤4/31<1 gives |Y|≤M=1. No noise, external contamination, or excluded lack of smoothness is used.

Put

\[
 I_0=\int_{-1}^1\psi(t)^2dt=\frac{4294967296}{9917826435},\qquad
 I_2=\int_{-1}^1t^2\psi(t)^2dt=I_0/35,\quad V_\rho=\int_0^1p^2=4/3.
\]

The exact squared L2(ρX) norm and limiting population eigenvalue for φj are

\[
 b_j^2=\int\phi_j^2p=2a_j^2\ell_jx_jI_0,
 \qquad
 \mu_j=\sqrt{2\pi}\int\phi_j^2p^2
 =4\sqrt{2\pi}a_j^2\ell_j(x_j^2I_0+\ell_j^2I_2).
\]

Consequently

\[
 \frac{b_j^2}{\mu_j}
 =\frac1{2\sqrt{2\pi}x_j(2241/2240)},\qquad
 \mu_j\asymp2^{-11j}.
\]

This density-dependent mismatch is the source of the failure: the local population risk controls p²-weighted error, while the advertised error uses p-weighted error.

### The actual population minimizer

Use exactly the paper's Gaussian weight, w_s(v)=s^(-3)exp(−v²/(2s²)). On HK, the population normal operator As in28 is diagonal in the φj basis because φj(x)φk(x)=0 for j≠k. Its diagonal entries are

\[
 A_j(s)=\int_0^1\phi_j(x)^2p(x)
 \left[\int_0^1w_s(u-x)(u-x)^2p(u)du\right]dx\ge0.
\]

For any x∈[0,1], substitute u=x+sz and use p(u)≤2x+2s|z|. Since ∫z²e^(−z²/2)dz=√(2π) and ∫|z|³e^(−z²/2)dz=4,

\[
 A_j(s)\le\mu_j+8sb_j^2. \tag{A}
\]

Let r_s=fρ,s−Asg, where fρ,s is30. The exact Taylor inequality and p≤2 give

\[
 \|r_s\|_{H_K}\le\kappa c'_\rho c_\rho s
 \int_{\mathbb R}|z|^3e^{-z^2/2}dz\le1024s.\tag{B}
\]

The genuine minimizer of27 is therefore

\[
 g_{\lambda,s}=(A_s+\lambda I)^{-1}A_sg+
 (A_s+\lambda I)^{-1}r_s.
\]

The first term has coefficient A_j/(A_j+λ) times1/j. Its bias has coefficient −λ/[j(A_j+λ)]. The remainder has HK norm≤1024s/λ, and hence L2(ρX) norm at most that quantity. Distinct φj are also orthogonal in L2(ρX).

### A finite, rigorously bounded violation of Proposition15

Choose j=20,

\[
 \lambda=\mu_{20}
 =\sqrt{2\pi}\,\frac{83}{2521912260907504525378102374907851709108631675058455042194826854400},
 \qquad s=\lambda^{16}.
\]

The printed restriction s≤min{c''ρλ^(1/τ),1} is met. It is met even if the apparent inverted constant c''ρ is corrected: with τ=1/8, the Gaussian bracket before the eighth power is below128, whereas λ<2^(−200) and s/λ^8=λ^8<2^(−1600).

EquationA gives A20(s)≤2λ. EquationB and orthogonality then imply

\[
 \frac{\|g_{\lambda,s}-g\|_\rho}{\sqrt\lambda}
 \ge\frac{b_{20}}{60\sqrt\lambda}-1024\lambda^{29/2}>6.99.\tag{C}
\]

In contrast, Proposition15's displayed upper bound, divided by √λ, is

\[
 \kappa^2c'_\rho J_3\frac{s}{\lambda^{3/2}}
 +2(V_\rho\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1/2}\|g\|_{H_K}
 \le512\lambda^{29/2}+\frac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt{(4/3)\sqrt{2\pi}}}<1.61.\tag{D}
\]

Both strict inequalities are certified by exact rational calculations in rate-counterexample.py. They use only 5/2<√(2π)<251/100, the exact integrals above, and squares of positive quantities. The first certificate launch had a Python reserved-keyword syntax error, corrected before any assertion was run; the saved completed certificate passes all assertions.

### Why this defeats the advertised main rate, beyond one constant

For the *same fixed* K,ρ,fρ above, let m_j=ceil(μ_j^(−27)) and use precisely Proposition9's parameter rule:

\[
 \lambda_m=m^{-1/27},\qquad s_m=2^{16}\lambda_m^8.
\]

Then λ_(m_j)/μ_j→1 and s_(m_j)/x_j→0. FromA–B, for all sufficiently large j,

\[
 \frac{\|g_{\lambda_m,s_m}-g\|_\rho}{\sqrt{\lambda_m}}
 \ge c\frac{2^{j/2}}j-o(1)\longrightarrow\infty.\tag{E}
\]

The empirical sample cannot restore the claimed O(√λm) rate by cancellation. Here is an independent sampling argument, without using the disputed L2 spectral steps. The population HK norm is uniformly bounded:

\[
 \|g_{\lambda,s}\|_{H_K}\le\|g\|_{H_K}+1024s/\lambda.
\]

Write the empirical estimating residual as Fm=m^(−2)Σi,j Hs(zi,zj), with

\[
 H_s((x,y),(u,v))=w_s(u-x)(u-x)K_x
 [v-y-(u-x)g_{\lambda,s}(x)].
\]

Since κ=1, |y|≤1, |u−x|≤1 and ||gλ,s||HK is bounded, Gaussian integration with p≤2 gives E||Hs||HK²≤C s^(−3). Replacing one observation affects at most2(m−1) pair terms. The Hilbert-space Efron–Stein inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give

\[
 E\|F_m-EF_m\|_{H_K}^2\le C/(ms^3).
\]

The empirical normal operator is positive on HK, so its regularized inverse has norm≤1/λ. The diagonal pair terms vanish, and EFm=(1−1/m)λgλ,s. Thus

\[
 E\|\widehat g_m-g_{\lambda,s}\|_{H_K}^2
 \le C/(m\lambda^2s^3)+C/m^2
 \le C'\lambda_m.\tag{F}
\]

The final equality uses m=λ_m^(−27) and s=2^16λ_m^8. The same bound holds for L2(ρX). By Markov's inequality, sampling error divided by √λm is tight, while the deterministic ratio inE diverges. This is an analytic asymptotic result, not a claimed simulation with the enormous m_j.

PDF14–15 defines LK using p(x)dρX(x)/Vρ, then treats it as a positive selfadjoint operator on L2(ρX) and asserts the usual RKHS square-root identity in that same metric. The natural measure for that identity is instead p dρX/Vρ. In this construction, applying the purported r=1/2 source condition in the unweighted L2(ρX) metric would require a series proportional to Σ2^j/j², which diverges, despite g∈HK. Thus the precise implication used to derive Proposition15 fails.

The positivity assertion itself already fails in a scalar exact example: take K(x,t)=1, the same p=2x, and h(x)=1−7x/5. Equation37 gives LKh=−1/20, while integral h dρX=1/15, so the L2(ρX) quadratic form is −1/300. This is supporting evidence of the same measure error, not a separate qualifying issue.

Changing to the p²-weighted metric changes the promised quantity; requiring a density bounded below excludes this legitimate smooth density and changes the stated theorem. Altering a Gaussian normalization factor, sign, or constant does not remove the exponential ratio inE. The estimator may still be consistent at a slower rate; no claim is made that consistency itself is impossible, nor that the historical gene-expression results are false.

**Why it matters.** An explicit central contribution is the error analysis showing that the learned gradient approaches the true gradient in the original data-distribution metric. The population theorem used to establish that analysis is false under its own assumptions, and a single fixed admissible example rules out the intended rate even after the equation's sign and constants are repaired. Repair requires a genuinely different theorem: for example an added density lower bound, a changed error metric, or a slower-rate analysis. The efficient solver and descriptive empirical illustrations do not establish the missing theoretical guarantee. This changes the assessment of a central contribution, rather than correcting notation while preserving its result.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the regularization proof, noticed that Equation37 uses p dρX/Vρ but the subsequent positive-operator/RKHS identity is asserted in L2(ρX). Investigated vanishing-density regions with disjoint smooth feature functions, then constructed an exact finite violation of Proposition15 and traced its consequence for the advertised sample rate.

**Verification method.** Read all31pages, including AppendicesA–C, and rechecked the original rendered assumptions, Proposition15, Equation37, source identification, Theorem19 and Proposition9 proof. Derived the population operator exactly in an orthogonal bump basis. Exact rational integral/inequality checks in unpublished audit files certify the finite contradiction, with saved `rate-certificate.json`. An independent reviewer checked the assumptions, exact moments, finite certificate and Hilbert Efron–Stein transfer argument; saved `fine-independent-assumption-results.json`. The growing-expression typography was rechecked at high resolution and explicitly excluded as the qualifying error. Continued through the empirical section, approximation proof and supplied MATLAB code after establishing the candidate.

**Confidence.** High. The finite contradiction has a wide certified margin and satisfies every stated hypothesis. The independent check agrees on both the population counterexample and the analytic sample-rate consequence. No historical rerun, numerical optimizer, or unobserved empirical leakage is needed for this theoretical finding.

Use exactly the paper's Gaussian weight, \(w_s(v)=s^{-3}\exp(-v^2/(2s^2))\). On \(\mathcal{H}_K\), the population normal operator As in28 is diagonal in the \(\varphi_j\) basis because \(\varphi_j(x)\varphi_k(x)=0\) for \(j\ne k\). Its diagonal entries are

For any \(x\in[0,1]\), substitute u=x+sz and use \(p(u)\le2x+2s|z|\). Since \(\int z^2e^{-z^2/2}\,dz=\sqrt{2\pi}\) and \(\int|z|^3e^{-z^2/2}\,dz=4\),

\[ A_j(s)\le\mu_j+8sb_j^2. \tag{A} \]

Let \(r_s=f_{\rho,s}-A_sg\), where \(f_{\rho,s}\) is30. The exact Taylor inequality and \(p\le2\) give

\[ \|r_s\|_{H_K}\le\kappa c'_\rho c_\rho s \int_{\mathbb R}|z|^3e^{-z^2/2}dz\le1024s.\tag{B} \]

The genuine minimizer of27 is therefore

\[ g_{\lambda,s}=(A_s+\lambda I)^{-1}A_sg+ (A_s+\lambda I)^{-1}r_s. \]

The first term has coefficient \(\frac{A_j}{A_j+\lambda}\) times1/j. Its bias has coefficient \(-\frac{\lambda}{j(A_j+\lambda)}\). The remainder has \(\mathcal{H}_K\) norm≤\(1024s/\lambda\), and hence \(L^2(\rho_X)\) norm at most that quantity. Distinct \(\varphi_j\) are also orthogonal in \(L^2(\rho_X)\).

A finite, rigorously bounded violation of Proposition15

Choose j=20,

\[ \lambda=\mu_{20} =\sqrt{2\pi}\,\frac{83}{2521912260907504525378102374907851709108631675058455042194826854400}, \qquad s=\lambda^{16}. \]

The printed restriction \(s\le\min\{c_\rho^{\prime\prime}\lambda^{1/\tau},1\}\) is met. It is met even if the apparent inverted constant c''\(\rho\) is corrected: with \(\tau=1/8\), the Gaussian bracket before the eighth power is below128, whereas \(\lambda<2^{-200}\) and \(s/\lambda^8=\lambda^8<2^{-1600}\).

EquationA gives \(A_{20}(s)\le2\lambda\). EquationB and orthogonality then imply

\[ \frac{\|g_{\lambda,s}-g\|_\rho}{\sqrt\lambda} \ge\frac{b_{20}}{60\sqrt\lambda}-1024\lambda^{29/2}>6.99.\tag{C} \]

In contrast, Proposition15's displayed upper bound, divided by \(\sqrt\lambda\), is

\[ \kappa^2c'_\rho J_3\frac{s}{\lambda^{3/2}} +2(V_\rho\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1/2}\|g\|_{H_K} \le512\lambda^{29/2}+\frac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt{(4/3)\sqrt{2\pi}}}<1.61.\tag{D} \]

Both strict inequalities are certified by exact rational calculations in rate-counterexample.py. They use only \(5/2<\sqrt{2\pi}<251/100\), the exact integrals above, and squares of positive quantities. Specifically \(\frac{b_{20}^2}{9\cdot20^2\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}}>49\), \(1024^2\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}^{29}<1/10000\), and the claimed leading coefficient is below8/5. The numerical output is illustrative; the rational inequalities and derivation establish the contradiction. The first certificate launch had a Python reserved-keyword syntax error, corrected before any assertion was run; the saved completed certificate passes all assertions.

Why this defeats the advertised main rate, beyond one constant

For the same fixed K,\(\rho\),\(f_\rho\) above, let \(m_j=\lceil\mu_j^{-27}\rceil\) and use precisely Proposition9's parameter rule:

\[ \lambda_m=m^{-1/27},\qquad s_m=2^{16}\lambda_m^8. \]

Then \(\lambda_{m_j}/\mu_j\to1\) and \(s_{m_j}/x_j\to0\). FromA–B, for all sufficiently large j,

\[ \frac{\|g_{\lambda_m,s_m}-g\|_\rho}{\sqrt{\lambda_m}} \ge c\frac{2^{j/2}}j-o(1)\longrightarrow\infty.\tag{E} \]

The empirical sample cannot restore the claimed O(\(\sqrt{\lambda_m}\)) rate by cancellation. Here is an independent sampling argument, without using the disputed L2 spectral steps. The population \(\mathcal{H}_K\) norm is uniformly bounded:

\[ \|g_{\lambda,s}\|_{H_K}\le\|g\|_{H_K}+1024s/\lambda. \]

Write the empirical estimating residual as \(F_m=m^{-2}\sum_{i,j}H_s(z_i,z_j)\), with

\[ H_s((x,y),(u,v))=w_s(u-x)(u-x)K_x [v-y-(u-x)g_{\lambda,s}(x)]. \]

Since \(\kappa=1\), \(|y|\le1\), \(|u-x|\le1\) and \(\lVert g_{\lambda,s}\rVert_{\mathcal H_K}\) is bounded, Gaussian integration with \(p\le2\) gives \(\mathbb{E}\lVert H_s\rVert_{\mathcal H_K}^2\le Cs^{-3}\). Replacing one observation affects at most2(m−1) pair terms. The Hilbert-space Efron–Stein inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give

\[ E\|F_m-EF_m\|_{H_K}^2\le C/(ms^3). \]

The empirical normal operator is positive on \(\mathcal{H}_K\), so its regularized inverse has norm≤\(1/\lambda\). The diagonal pair terms vanish, and \(\mathbb{E}F_m=(1-1/m)\lambda g_{\lambda,s}\). Thus

\[ E\|\widehat g_m-g_{\lambda,s}\|_{H_K}^2 \le C/(m\lambda^2s^3)+C/m^2 \le C'\lambda_m.\tag{F} \]

The final equality uses \(m=\lambda_m^{-27}\) and \(s=2^{16}\lambda_m^8\). The same bound holds for \(L^2(\rho_X)\). By Markov's inequality, sampling error divided by \(\sqrt{\lambda_m}\) is tight, while the deterministic ratio inE diverges. For each fixed C and fixed \(\delta\) (e.g.\(\delta\)=1/4), the probability that \(\lVert\widehat g_m-g\rVert_\rho\) exceeds C√λm tends to1 along \(m_j\). No finite \(C_{\rho,K}\) recovers the intended decaying main rate. This is an analytic asymptotic result, not a claimed simulation with the enormous \(m_j\).

Failed proof step and scope

PDF14–15 defines LK using \(p(x)\,d\rho_X(x)/V_\rho\), then treats it as a positive selfadjoint operator on \(L^2(\rho_X)\) and asserts the usual RKHS square-root identity in that same metric. The natural measure for that identity is instead \(p\,d\rho_X/V_\rho\). In this construction, applying the purported r=1/2 source condition in the unweighted \(L^2(\rho_X)\) metric would require a series proportional to \(\sum_j2^j/j^2\), which diverges, despite \(g\in\mathcal H_K\). Thus the precise implication used to derive Proposition15 fails.

The positivity assertion itself already fails in a scalar exact example: take \(K(x,t)\)=1, the same p=2x, and \(h(x)\)=1−7x/5. Equation37 gives \(L_Kh=-1/20\), while integral \(h\,d\rho_X=1/15\), so the \(L^2(\rho_X)\) quadratic form is −1/300. This is supporting evidence of the same measure error, not a separate qualifying issue.

Changing to the p²-weighted metric changes the promised quantity; requiring a density bounded below excludes this legitimate smooth density and changes the stated theorem. Altering a Gaussian normalization factor, sign, or constant does not remove the exponential ratio inE. The estimator may still be consistent at a slower rate; no claim is made that consistency itself is impossible, nor that the historical gene-expression results are false.

Why it matters.

An explicit central contribution is the error analysis showing that the learned gradient approaches the true gradient in the original data-distribution metric. The population theorem used to establish that analysis is false under its own assumptions, and a single fixed admissible example rules out the intended rate even after the equation's sign and constants are repaired. Repair requires a genuinely different theorem: for example an added density lower bound, a changed error metric, or a slower-rate analysis. The efficient solver and descriptive empirical illustrations do not establish the missing theoretical guarantee. This changes the assessment of a central contribution, rather than correcting notation while preserving its result.

Discovery method.

While tracing the regularization proof, noticed that Equation37 uses \(p\,d\rho_X/V_\rho\) but the subsequent positive-operator/RKHS identity is asserted in \(L^2(\rho_X)\). Investigated vanishing-density regions with disjoint smooth feature functions, then constructed an exact finite violation of Proposition15 and traced its consequence for the advertised sample rate.

Continued through the empirical section, approximation proof and supplied MATLAB code after establishing the candidate.

Confidence.

High. The finite contradiction has a wide certified margin and satisfies every stated hypothesis. The independent check agrees on both the population counterexample and the analytic sample-rate consequence. No historical rerun, numerical optimizer, or unobserved empirical leakage is needed for this theoretical finding.

The full derivation is also saved in unpublished audit files; the certificate and independent assumption checks are in the same directory. linear-system-check.py/linear-results.json document the separate positive checks of the solver and full-rank reduction, rather than attributing those methods' failure to this issue.
